# The Value of Disagreement

## Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like: a room full of people who started with different views and ended, through discussion and persuasion, in harmony. Everyone nods. Someone writes up the summary. The meeting ends with a feeling of warmth and accomplishment. We did it, we agree.

But this picture deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, is not always a sign that a group has done its thinking well. Sometimes agreement is genuine—the discussion surfaced the real considerations, and everyone's judgment converged on the same conclusion. But sometimes agreement is a mask. It can hide the fact that people are uncertain and don't want to admit it. It can hide that some participants are deferring to the loudest voice or the most senior person in the room. It can hide that the group never actually examined the assumptions underneath the plan it just approved. And it can hide the fact that "agreement" means different things to different people—that three people who all said "yes" were imagining three different things.
